title: Nervous System as a System
think_prompt: A receptor detects a change, but how does the correct effector know what to do?
definition: The nervous system coordinates rapid communication between receptors and effectors.
description: This subunit views the nervous system as an information-processing system. Information is received from receptors, processed within the nervous system, and commands are sent to effectors to produce suitable responses.
key_points: Receptor → Nervous system → Effector|Input → Processing → Output|Rapid coordination
image_description: 16:9 Grade 11 science overview infographic. Show a human figure with a sensory receptor receiving a stimulus on the left, the brain and spinal cord as a central processing area in the middle, and a muscle or gland producing an action on the right. Use clear directional arrows to communicate Receptor → Nervous System → Effector and the broader idea Receive → Process → Act. Clean modern educational style, uncluttered, suitable for a classroom smart board.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the three broad stages shown in the visual before revealing the system model.
quick_check: What is the main role of the nervous system between a receptor and an effector?
answer: It receives information from receptors, processes or coordinates it, and sends commands to effectors.

title: Why Do We Need the Nervous System?
memory_badge: Fast communication keeps the body coordinated.
think_prompt: What would happen if receptors could detect danger but could not quickly communicate with the rest of the body?
definition: The nervous system provides rapid communication and coordination between different parts of the body.
description: Receptors detect changes, but detection alone cannot produce a useful response. The body needs a system that rapidly carries information, coordinates it, and directs the correct effector.
image_description: 16:9 educational scenario visual. Show a student touching a hot object. On the left, a skin receptor detects heat; in the centre, a simplified nervous-system pathway carries information rapidly toward the central nervous system; on the right, arm muscles withdraw the hand. Emphasize the need for fast communication rather than detailed neuron anatomy. Realistic Grade 11 science style with clear directional flow.
interaction_instruction: Ask students what would fail if communication between receptor and effector were delayed or absent.
quick_check: Why is the nervous system necessary for coordination?
answer: Because it provides rapid communication that links receptors with effectors and allows suitable responses.
remarks: Establishes need and role without repeating SU01 definitions

title: Receiving Information — Input
memory_badge: Input begins when receptors detect change.
think_prompt: How does information about a change enter the nervous system?
definition: Receptors detect stimuli and provide sensory information to the nervous system.
description: The first stage of nervous coordination is input. A receptor detects a change and information is carried toward the nervous system. This gives the system information about what is happening inside or outside the body.
key_points: Receptor|Sensory input|Information enters nervous system|Input stage
image_description: 16:9 process illustration focused on input. Show three simple examples on the left such as bright light reaching the eye, sound reaching the ear, and heat touching skin. Arrows from the receptors converge toward a simplified nervous-system silhouette on the right. Highlight the direction of information entering the system. Avoid detailed neuron structures. Clean smart-board infographic.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to point out where the information starts and the direction in which it travels.
quick_check: What provides the input to the nervous system?
answer: Information detected by receptors provides the input to the nervous system.
remarks: Input stage of the information-processing model

title: Processing Information
memory_badge: The nervous system decides how the body should respond.
think_prompt: Once information reaches the nervous system, what must happen before an effector can act?
definition: Processing is the coordination of incoming information so that an appropriate response can be organized.
description: The nervous system acts as the coordinating centre between input and action. It receives information from receptors, processes or integrates that information, and determines the command that should be sent to the appropriate effector.
image_description: 16:9 educational concept visual. Place a simplified brain and spinal cord at the centre as the processing region. Several input arrows from sensory receptors enter from the left, while one or more command arrows leave toward effectors on the right. Use a clean central processing visual metaphor such as sorting incoming signals into an appropriate outgoing command, but do not show computer hardware. Grade 11 biology infographic style.
interaction_instruction: Present an input example and ask students to predict what kind of command the nervous system should organize.
quick_check: What happens during the processing stage of nervous coordination?
answer: The nervous system receives and coordinates incoming information and organizes an appropriate response.

title: Sending Commands — Output
think_prompt: After the nervous system processes information, where must the command go?
definition: The output stage occurs when the nervous system sends a command to an effector.
description: After processing, the nervous system directs information to an appropriate effector. Muscles or glands then carry out the action, producing the observable response.
key_points: Command from nervous system|Effector|Muscle or gland|Output stage|Response
image_description: 16:9 process diagram focused on output. Show a simplified central nervous system on the left sending a clear directional signal to two possible effectors on the right: a skeletal muscle producing movement and a gland producing secretion. Emphasize that the command leaves the nervous system and reaches a specific effector. Clean educational illustration with minimal labels.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to match example nervous-system commands with the correct type of effector: muscle or gland.
quick_check: What receives the output from the nervous system?
answer: An effector, such as a muscle or gland, receives the command and produces the response.

title: Nervous System as an Information-Processing System
think_prompt: Can the whole role of the nervous system be summarized using only three stages?
definition: The nervous system can be modelled as an information-processing system with input, processing, and output.
description: Receptors provide input, the nervous system processes and coordinates the information, and commands sent to effectors produce output. This three-stage model summarizes the role of the nervous system as a complete coordinating system.
key_points: Input = receptor information|Processing = nervous system|Output = effector action|Receptor → Nervous system → Effector
image_description: 16:9 clean systems diagram with three large horizontal zones: INPUT → PROCESSING → OUTPUT. In INPUT show a receptor detecting a stimulus; in PROCESSING show a simplified brain and spinal cord; in OUTPUT show a muscle or gland acting. Beneath or within the same visual, map the biological pathway Receptor → Nervous System → Effector to the three system stages. Large readable smart-board composition with simple icons and strong directional arrows.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to place receptor, nervous system, and effector under Input, Processing, and Output.
quick_check: Complete the system model: Receptor → ______ → Effector.

title: Apply the Whole System
memory_badge: Trace the information, not just the action.
think_prompt: A bright light suddenly enters your eyes. Can you trace the information from detection to action?
definition: A nervous-coordination pathway can be analysed by identifying input, processing, and output.
description: Use a new situation to identify the receptor providing input, the nervous system processing the information, and the effector carrying out the output. The same system model can be applied to many rapid body responses.
key_points: Identify input|Identify processing|Identify output|Apply system model
image_description: 16:9 application scene. Show a student exposed to sudden bright light. Light reaches the eye, an arrow carries information toward a simplified brain or central nervous system, and a command returns toward an eye-related effector response. Keep the visual conceptual and suitable for students to infer Input → Processing → Output without printing the answers. Clean realistic Grade 11 educational style.
interaction_instruction: Ask students to identify the receptor/input, nervous-system processing stage, and effector/output from the visual before revealing the answer.
quick_check: In a nervous response, what are the three system stages?
answer: Input from receptors → Processing by the nervous system → Output through effectors.
remarks: Final retrieval/application scene; ready to bridge to SU03 Neuron
